entities.name: Hydarnes II
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Hydarnes II, also known as Hydarnes the Younger, distinguished himself as a pivotal Persian commander within the Achaemenid Empire during the 5th century BCE, a period defined by the epochal Greco-Persian Wars. As the son of Hydarnes, a prominent satrap and one of the seven conspirators who elevated Darius I to the throne, Hydarnes II inherited a legacy of military and political influence. His significance is indelibly linked to his decisive role in the Persian victory at the Battle of Thermopylae in 480 BCE, where his strategic acumen directly contributed to the outflanking and annihilation of the Spartan-led Greek forces.

His most celebrated action occurred during the second Persian invasion of Greece under Xerxes I. At Thermopylae, while the main Persian army faced fierce resistance from the Greek hoplites in the narrow pass, Hydarnes II was tasked with leading the elite Immortals along the Anopaia path, a treacherous mountain trail. Guided by a local Malian named Ephialtes, Hydarnes successfully navigated his contingent to the rear of the Greek positions, a maneuver that rendered the Greek defensive strategy untenable and sealed the fate of Leonidas's Spartans.

The strategic success orchestrated by Hydarnes II at Thermopylae had profound immediate consequences, opening the path for the Persian advance into central Greece and the subsequent sacking of Athens. While ultimately the Persian invasion was repelled at Salamis and Plataea, Hydarnes's tactical brilliance at Thermopylae showcased the sophisticated military capabilities of the Achaemenid Empire and forced the Greeks to adapt their defensive strategies. His actions underscored the critical importance of intelligence and flank maneuvers in ancient warfare, a lesson that resonated through subsequent military engagements.
